title: Lecture #31: Java Collection Interface Deep Dive
topics: Bulk operations: addAll, removeAll, retainAll, containsAll

questions.question: What is the difference between `Collection` and `Collections` in `java.util`?
options: `Collection` is a class you instantiate directly; `Collections` is the interface it implements
`Collection` is the root interface for lists, sets and queues; `Collections` is a utility class of static helper methods
They are two names for the same interface; `Collections` is just the older name
`Collection` holds single elements; `Collections` is the interface for key-value data
questions.explanation: `Collection<E>` is an interface (extending `Iterable<E>`) implemented via List, Set and Queue classes, so you write `Collection<Integer> c = new ArrayList<>();`. `Collections` is a separate final utility class with static methods that operate on collections. You can never write `new Collection<>()` because it is an interface, and key-value data is `Map`, not `Collections`.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: true true 2
true true 1
false false 1
true false 1
questions.explanation: `boolean add(E e)` returns true only if the collection changed. The HashSet accepts the first 5, but the second `add(5)` is a duplicate, so the set is unchanged and `add` returns false; the size stays 1. On an ArrayList both calls would return true — the return value is how the Collection API reports whether the call had an effect.

questions.question: You have a collection of user IDs who opened an email and want to keep in it only the IDs that also appear in a second collection of users who clicked a link (an intersection). Which single Collection method does this in place?
options: `opened.retainAll(clicked)`
`opened.removeAll(clicked)`
`opened.containsAll(clicked)`
`opened.addAll(clicked)`
questions.explanation: `retainAll(c)` removes every element that is NOT in `c`, leaving the intersection — the lecture labels it exactly that. `removeAll(c)` does the opposite (removes the common elements, a difference), `containsAll` only answers true/false without changing anything, and `addAll` produces a union-like result.

questions.topic: Bulk operations: addAll, removeAll, retainAll, containsAll
questions.question: After these bulk operations, what is printed?
options: [1, 3, 5] false
[7] true
questions.explanation: After `addAll` the list is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]; `removeAll` drops 2, 4 and 6, leaving [1, 3, 5]. `retainAll` keeps only elements also in [1, 3, 5, 7] — all of 1, 3, 5 are there, so nothing is removed and it returns false (it never adds 7). Like `add`/`remove`, the bulk methods return whether the collection changed.

questions.question: A `Collection<Student>` holds `new Student(1, "Aditya")`. Later `students.contains(new Student(1, "Aditya"))` returns false, although the data is identical. `Student` does not override any `Object` methods. What is the cause?
options: `contains` only works for wrapper types like Integer and String, not for user classes
`contains` decides membership using `equals()`; without an override `Object.equals` compares references, and the two Student objects are different instances
`contains` compares objects with `compareTo()`, so `Student` must implement Comparable
The collection must be iterated manually because `contains` only checks the first element
questions.explanation: `boolean contains(Object o)` walks the elements and asks `o.equals(element)`. The inherited `Object.equals` is reference equality, so a newly created but identical Student is not found. Overriding `equals()` (and `hashCode()` for hash-based collections) fixes it; `compareTo` is not what `contains` uses.

questions.question: The lecture converts a `Collection<Integer>` with `Integer[] arr = c.toArray(new Integer[0]);` instead of `(Integer[]) c.toArray()`. Why?
options: Because `toArray()` without arguments returns only the first element
Because `toArray(new Integer[0])` always returns an empty array, which is faster
Because the no-argument version sorts the elements, while the typed version keeps their order
Because `toArray()` returns an `Object[]` whose runtime type is not `Integer[]`, so the cast fails with `ClassCastException`; the typed version returns an array of the requested runtime type
questions.explanation: `Object[] toArray()` creates an `Object[]`, and arrays remember their runtime type, so casting it to `Integer[]` throws `ClassCastException`. `<T> T[] toArray(T[] a)` uses the given array's type; if the array is too small (like length 0) it allocates a new `Integer[]` of the right size and fills it. It does not return an empty array and neither version sorts.

questions.question: Given `Collection<Integer> c = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));`, which call does NOT compile?
options: `c.get(0)`
`c.isEmpty()`
`c.containsAll(List.of(1, 2))`
`c.toArray(new Integer[0])`
questions.explanation: The compiler only allows methods of the declared type `Collection`, and `Collection` has no index-based `get` because sets and queues are not indexed — even though the object is really an ArrayList. `isEmpty`, `containsAll` and `toArray(T[])` are all declared in `Collection`. Declaring the variable as `List<Integer>` would make `get(0)` available.

questions.question: `Collection` declares `equals(Object o)` and `hashCode()`, and each sub-interface defines what equality means. Which statement is correct?
options: An ArrayList and a LinkedList are never equal, because `equals` first checks that both objects have the same class
Two lists are equal whenever they contain the same elements, in any order
An ArrayList and a LinkedList with the same elements in the same order are equal, but a List is never equal to a Set even if they hold the same elements
Collection `equals` compares references like `==` unless the programmer overrides it
questions.explanation: The List contract says two lists are equal if they have the same elements in the same order, regardless of implementation class, so `ArrayList [1, 2]` equals `LinkedList [1, 2]`. The Set contract compares sets only with other sets (order ignored), and a List is never equal to a Set. The JDK collections already override `equals`, so it is not reference comparison, and order does matter for lists.

questions.question: Both variables hold an `ArrayList` with the same contents. What does this print?
questions.explanation: Overloads are chosen at compile time from the declared type. `Collection` only has `remove(Object)`, so `c.remove(3)` autoboxes 3 and removes the value 3, giving [1, 2, 4]. `List` adds `remove(int index)`, which matches the `int` argument exactly, so `l.remove(3)` removes the element at index 3 (the value 4), giving [1, 2, 3].

questions.question: `Collection<Number> nums = new ArrayList<>(); nums.addAll(List.of(1, 2));` compiles, but with `Collection<Integer> ints = new ArrayList<>();` and `List<Number> mixed = List.of(1, 2.5);`, the call `ints.addAll(mixed)` does not. Given the signature in the lecture, what explains this?
options: `addAll` only accepts arguments of exactly the same type, `Collection<E>`
`addAll` is declared `addAll(Collection<? super E> c)`, so it only accepts collections of supertypes of E
`addAll` accepts any `Collection<?>`, so the failure must come from autoboxing 2.5
`addAll` is declared `addAll(Collection<? extends E> c)`: a `List<Integer>` is a valid producer for a `Collection<Number>`, but a `List<Number>` is not a `Collection<? extends Integer>`
questions.explanation: Following PECS, `addAll` reads from its argument, so it is declared `Collection<? extends E>`: for E = Number, a `List<Integer>` qualifies. For E = Integer, a `List<Number>` could contain a Double, so the compiler rejects it. Methods like `removeAll`/`retainAll` take `Collection<?>` because they only compare with `equals`, but `addAll` must ensure type safety of what it inserts.
